claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys generally face a strength–ductility trade-off.
Processing-induced grain refinement can simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Control of phase architecture can simultaneously improve strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Spark plasma sintering can produce the grain refinement and phase control required for the proposed improvement.
Additive manufacturing can produce the grain refinement and phase control required for the proposed improvement.
The proposed improvement should hold at room temperature.
The proposed improvement should hold at elevated temperatures.
A single-phase BCC structure is a candidate controlled phase state for balancing strength and ductility.
A combination of BCC and Laves phases is a candidate controlled phase state for balancing strength and ductility.
A fine multiphase microstructure containing soft FCC and hard BCC/B2 phases can provide high strength and high ductility.
Grain refinement improves both strength and ductility by reducing obstacles to dislocation movement.
Improved grain-boundary cohesion contributes to simultaneous enhancement of strength and ductility.
The intervention will increase strength relative to current eutectic high-entropy-alloy baselines.
The intervention will increase ductility relative to current eutectic high-entropy-alloy baselines.
The intervention can improve both properties without a significant strength–ductility trade-off.
Current eutectic high-entropy alloys have limited strength and ductility because of microstructural and phase-composition limitations.
The effectiveness of the intervention depends on alloy composition, processing conditions, and testing environment.
The magnitude of the expected strength and ductility improvements is unknown.
The optimal processing conditions are unknown.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes higher strength partly to reducing obstacles to dislocation movement, whereas reducing such obstacles ordinarily facilitates plastic flow and does not coherently explain the claimed strength increase.

The mediator presents single-phase BCC as a candidate for the desired balance, while the cited rationale for simultaneous strength and ductility instead relies on a fine soft-FCC/hard-BCC multiphase architecture; cited records also describe limitations associated with single-phase or brittle BCC states.
